passages.text: Leveraging COVID-19 to modernise depression care for VA primary care populations: protocol for a sequential explanatory mixed method evaluation
Abstract
Background

The Veterans Health Administration (VA) integrated mental and physical health services to better detect and treat depression. Primary care nurses conduct screening annually. Clinicians, including Primary Care Mental Health Integration (PCMHI) specialists, follow-up as needed for treatment. Depression detection and management processes are complex, involve multilevel stakeholders, and are subject to significant disruption from COVID-19 and from the resulting expansion of telehealth, aiming to preserve care access. This study aimed to examine whether the COVID-19 pandemic worsened depression-related care quality and/or patient outcomes (eg, suicide).
Methods

Given hypothesised care disruption (lowered care quality) during COVID-19, we will first assess the VA population's trajectory from a new positive depression (and suicide risk) screen to appropriate treatment (ie, medication, therapy) in the Fiscal Year 2019-2323. We will also examine the changing mix of virtual and in-person depression care delivered. Second, we will use interrupted time series analyses to explore the extent to which psychiatric emergency visits and hospitalisations may be mitigated by clinician detection of depression. As well as compare mental health-related mortality rates between patients detected and not detected to have depression. Subanalyses will reveal where (eg, clinics with low PCMHI access) and for whom (eg, minorities) detection does not systematically occur, and downstream negative sequelae, to guide future intervention. Finally, we will interview 40 veterans, half of whom were detected and half not detected to have depression and 40 VA primary care and PCMHI providers about changes brought on by the pandemic and the expansion of virtual care across three VA facilities. In addition to contextualising disrupted care findings, qualitative data will help identify best practices on patient-to-provider and provider-to-provider interactions in hybrid in-person/telehealth depression care models.
Ethics and dissemination

Ethics approval was granted by the VA Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System Institutional Review Board. Alongside journal publications, dissemination activities include briefings to our policy and operational partners, and presentations to clinical, research and policy-oriented audiences.
STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY
A key strength of the study is our methods in tracking population-based quality metrics for depression care among the entire VA population nationally.

Another strength is our mixed methods approach, which allows us to leverage multidisciplinary expertise from primary care-based teams to contextualise quantitative findings and gather best practices on patient-to-provider and provider-to-provider (eg, handoffs) interactions in hybrid (in-person/virtual) depression care models.

As with all observational research studies, establishing causal relationships is precluded; identifying and tracking outcomes among patients with positive depression screens is inherently limited by the accuracy of coding within medical records and administrative data.
Introduction

Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and the most common psychiatric illness observed in the Veterans Health Administration (VA), affecting one in five patients. It also contributes substantially to the pandemic-related mental health crisis. 42% report anxiety/depression symptoms, with more than 1/10 unable to receive mental health counselling. Given widespread social and economic disruption, COVID-19 has been 'the perfect storm' for veterans, especially those with pre-existing conditions. Veterans, at baseline, have 50% higher prevalence of depression, as well as a higher risk for loneliness/social isolation than civilians. The extent of pandemic-related disruptions in care and disease prevalence, specifically among VA patients, is unclear, however. Estimates have been reported to be as high as double among veterans as surveyed by non-profit organisations (eg, Wounded Warrior Project), while others have reported estimates that are closer to those of the general population. Many fear the downstream effects of pandemic disruptions on veterans since depression has long been associated with increased overall mortality. Veterans rely more heavily on and preferentially seek treatment from the VA mental healthcare infrastructure, as compared with the private sector. However, high demand for depression care may have been coupled with low supply in the pandemic, given anecdotal constraints on medical services (eg, staffing shortages, staff strain and reduced care access).

Primary care and mental health integration can effectively treat depression, but access gaps exist. Primary care encounters offer opportunities for patients to newly engage in depression screening, medication management, brief therapy and/or referral. Many who are detected with depression are identified first in primary care, including those who are reluctant to seek mental health specialists. The VA has mandated annual depression screening for over two decades, achieving near-universal screening rates among clinics nationally, and has newly begun universal suicide risk screening in primary care. Growing need for improved access to high-quality depression treatment led to the development of collaborative care management models in primary care, which is now supported by over 79 clinical trials. The VA has implemented this and other models of integrated care nationally through the Primary Care Mental Health Integration (PCMHI) initiative and has demonstrated positive programmatic outcomes. VA primary care and integrated mental health providers (including nurse care managers) are available to collaboratively manage and treat the majority of veterans with mild-to-moderate depression using evidence-based psychotherapy and medication. Specifically, the VA uses colocated collaborative care (CCC), which embeds PCMHI providers who are available for warm handoffs from primary care and/or collaborative care management (CoCM), which offers phone-based depression care management by mental health-trained RNs. More intensive services (eg, Residential Rehabilitation Treatment Programmes, Mental Health Intensive Case Management Programme) are available for patients with severe symptoms or complex conditions through traditional mental health speciality referrals. Yet, only ~1/3 of VA primary care patients newly detected with depression receive timely follow-up (>=3 visits within 3 months). With the COVID-19 onset, PCMHI services have dropped by 18%, partially mitigated by the expansion of telehealth, potentially worsening overall depression care quality.

To bridge access gaps widened by COVID-19, telehealth has emerged to connect patients to providers across distance (eg, synchronous video visits) and/or time (eg, secure electronic messages via patient portals). As the largest integrated healthcare system in the country, VA was an early adopter of telehealth and had secure messaging, telephone care, e-consults and video-to-home visits already available prior to the pandemic. Consequently, telehealth visits skyrocketed and partially offset COVID-related reductions in overall healthcare utilisation in the VA and elsewhere. Yet, telehealth is not without limitations, nor is it a panacea for all care delivery disruptions during the pandemic. At the patient level, there are several notable disparities in telehealth use related to rurality, age and race-ethnicity, similarly observed within the VA. At the provider and system level, telehealth adoption and implementation vary across VA settings and are essential to monitor as part of mental healthcare delivery. The COVID-19 pandemic provides an unparalleled opportunity to close evidence gaps in telehealth use. For example, we can now examine patient experiences from those who may not have initially elected telehealth, unlike prior research reports on satisfaction, mostly from those who opted into telehealth trials. More importantly, we can now close the evidence gaps surrounding depression care models that deliver a combination of virtual and in-person services for Veteran populations (eg, for whom, under what conditions) through a unique opportunity for observational study in a national disaster.

To improve virtual and in-person services for the VA primary care population during recovery, we will examine how the pandemic disrupted depression care delivery mechanisms (including expanded telehealth) and impacted Veteran health outcomes. We hypothesise (1) increased demand for high-quality depression care among veterans, and (2) decreased supply of appropriate disease detection/management (lower quality) in the VA. We will adapt Fortney et al's access framework to guide study variable selection. This framework reconceptualises care access and quality in the digital age by accounting for both in-person and virtual healthcare encounters. It comprehensively considers patient, provider, health system and community determinants of access across five dimensions: geographical, temporal, financial, cultural and digital. (figure 1) To our knowledge, this will be the first national study to assess the entire VA population's trajectory from a new positive depression (and suicide risk) screen to guideline-concordant follow-up and treatment (ie, medication, psychotherapy), making this a novel method. Our specific aims are (1) to examine engagement in guideline-concordant care for depression (virtual or in-person) following screening, before and during the pandemic; (2) to compare psychiatric emergency/hospital visits and mortality from suicide between veterans who screened positive and were detected versus not detected to have depression by clinicians and (3) to understand VA patients' and providers' current perspectives on addressing new depressive episodes using virtual and in-person modalities during the pandemic and eventual recovery.
Access framework for this study adapted from Fortney et al. VA, Veterans Health Administration.
Methods

We propose a sequential explanatory mixed methods evaluation of pandemic-related disruptions to VA depression care and outcomes. Study variables from our two quantitative aims and one qualitative aim map onto Fortney et al's access framework. Aims 1 and 2 employ a national retrospective cohort study design to understand how much, for whom and where depression care was disrupted using existing VA administrative, medical and pharmacy databases. In Aim 3, qualitative data from veterans (identified in Aims 1 and 2) and VA providers in 3 VA sites (Greater Los Angeles (GLA), Syracuse and Durham) on experiences with using virtual and in-person depression care modalities will be used to help interpret and contextualise disrupted care findings from our quantitative aims. We will then be well poised to test hypotheses in model enhancements (eg, new depression treatments), and to gather and disseminate best practices on patient-to-provider and provider-to-provider (eg, handoffs) interactions in hybrid depression care models during the pandemic and recovery.
Patient and public involvement

We directly engage veteran patients in two ways: (1) GLA and Syracuse Veteran Engagement Group guided research design (eg, patient recruitment and interview questions) and dissemination to lay audiences; (2) veterans will provide input during interviews regarding their experiences with depression care access, quality and outcomes during the pandemic.
Quantitative data collection
Setting

For Aims 1 and 2, we anticipate a national sample of VA patients to include 5-6M veterans cared for in over 1000 clinics (with less than half serving 5000+ patients annually). Based on our prior analyses, VA primary care patients tend to be 65+ years old (48%), White (68%) and men (91%). Since depression screening is mandated annually, documentation rates in primary care clinics are 96%. Among patients without a prior diagnosis and not already receiving medication treatment, ~8% newly screened positive for depression each year.
Study cohort

Our retrospective cohort study will include all veterans eligible to be screened for depression (via Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)) in any VA facility nationally in Fiscal Year (FY) 2019-2023, using the VA Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW) administrative, medical and pharmacy databases. We will exclude the handful of VA Medical Centres that have transitioned to the Oracle Cerner medical record system. First, we will include patients who screened positive for depression in primary care clinics (which conduct 75%+ of screening) by scoring >=3 on the PHQ-2 (72% sensitivity and 85% specificity), as per VA Clinical Practice Guidelines for Major Depressive Disorder. Second, we will restrict to cohort patients with a new episode of depression. New episodes are defined as not having a depression diagnosis (per International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10) in online supplemental 1) or engaged in PCMHI and mental healthcare (completed appropriate treatment, table 1) in the past 6 months (figure 2). Finally, we will identify those who were detected by a clinician as having clinically significant depression. Detection is defined as clinicians coding depression diagnoses or prescribing antidepressants within 12 months (onlinesupplemental 1  2).

Measures

Dependent variables (table 1): Aim 1 outcome measures build on an established method for generating population-based metrics. Measures were based on depression care literature, prior quality measures from the VA and the National Committee for Quality Assurance (eg, Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set), and depression guidelines. In a prior study, a modified Delphi panel of VA and non-VA experts agreed on each measure. We will construct three measures for meeting guideline-concordant depression follow-up and treatment, either in person or telehealth (onlinesupplemental 35).

Aim 2 will examine psychiatric emergency visits and hospitalisations as a proxy for severe disease, either at a VA or non-VA facility (paid for by the VA). Traditional PHQ-9 scores and quality of life indicators are not available for population-level analyses. We will classify admitting diagnoses by psychiatric/substance use disorder (eg, primary diagnosis of suicidal ideation, ICD-10 code R45.851). We will examine mortality categorised by cause of death: all-cause (previously found to be 45.1/1000 person-years), COVID-19 (ICD-10 code U07.1) and suicide (X60-84, Y87.0, U03). The VA and US Department of Defense (DoD) Mortality Data Repository includes date and cause of death for all VA users, per annual VA-DoD searches of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Death Index.

Independent variables/covariates: guided by Fortney et al.'s access framework, quantitative data analyses will comprehensively examine patient and clinic characteristics related to engagement in quality depression care and available in VA's CDW and other existing administrative, medical and pharmacy databases (box 1).

Patient: we will examine patient-level variables previously found to be associated with engagement in quality depression care: patient age, sex, race-ethnicity (eg, non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic), marital status and health diagnoses. Socioeconomic factors will be approximated by the US census-based measures of socioeconomic status (eg, Area Deprivation Index). To measure the need for care, we will use ICD-10 codes in outpatient and inpatient visits to monitor other psychiatric diagnoses (eg, anxiety, PTSD, alcohol and substance use disorders, serious mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder)) over time to account for potential changes in psychiatric disease base rates related to the pandemic. ICD-10 codes will also allow us to calculate the Charlson Comorbidity Index to risk-adjust physical health for each patient. Actual measures of financial and geographical access to care will be measured by the need for copayment (patients may be eligible for VA care due to a service-connected disability or exempt from copayment for having low financial means) and travel distance from home to clinic.

Clinic: we will adjust for organisation-level factors that may influence depression care access and quality. They include whether patients' assigned clinics were community- versus hospital-based, rural versus urban location and assigned 5000 versus <5000 primary care patients. In particular, we will also examine the exposure of (1) PCMHI access/reach (eg, clinician staffing, patients with same-day PCMHI referrals, clinic proportion of primary care patients seen by PCMHI providers), which are both important VA performance metrics, and (2) telehealth adoption (eg, % telehealth use). Albeit imperfect, exposure measures offer approximations of available clinic resources and staffing to deliver timely, accessible VA depression care, which we will further explore in subsequent qualitative analyses. We hypothesise that PCMHI and telehealth exposure will allow for higher depression care quality. For example, clinics with higher baseline rates of same-day PCMHI referrals will provide timelier follow-up after a positive screen than clinics with lower rates.
Data analysis

In Aim 1, we will build depression measures to describe population-level care quality. First, we will use univariate analyses to describe all study variables in the veteran population. Bivariate comparisons by patient and clinic covariates with the primary outcomes (depression care quality metric met versus not met) will be compared using chi2 tests. Next, we will use multivariable models (ie, generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) framework) to examine associations between depression measures and both patient and clinic covariates, which will facilitate our understanding of what may predict high-quality care. Logistic regressions will be used, given the dichotomous nature of our quality outcomes. To examine for potential disruption over time, we will also conduct individual-level interrupted time series analyses through segmented logistic regressions on repeated quarterly observations of depression care quality over 54 months (1 October 2018-31 March 2023). The time series will be divided into three segments: (1) pre-COVID (1 October 2018-15 March 2020, VA COVID-19 guidelines for clinic operations thereafter), (2) onset and multiple waves of COVID-19 (16 March 2020-30 September 2021, when full U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of a COVID-19 vaccine was obtained), (3) continued re-expansion of in-person medical services to the end of the observation period (1 October 2021-31 March 2023). Furthermore, we will include healthcare system fixed effects to account for invariant organisational characteristics. Standard errors will be estimated that account for the clustering of patients within clinics. Patient random effects may be included if it is noted that a large proportion of patients have multiple and, therefore, non-independent observations during the four study years. A three-level model will allow for the nesting of multiple patients within a clinic and for the correlation among clinics within a healthcare system. The intra-class correlation (ICC) coefficient will be examined to assess the magnitude of association at the VA healthcare system's level and at the individual clinic level, though the GLMM will include an appropriately chosen covariance structure to account for clustering. Even low values of ICC may inflate the Type I error; thus, incorporating random effects preserves overall Type I error rates for hypothesis tests. For our projected sample size of 1 25 000 patients with new depressive episodes (among the entire VA primary care population), we will have a power far in excess of 0.90 to detect ORs of as little as 1.03 between patient and clinic covariates (including exposure variables) and depression care quality for a two-tailed test at the 0.05 level. This study is overpowered to demonstrate clinically meaningful relationships, so we have prespecified hypotheses on significant differences. We will manage and analyse data using SAS V.9.4 and/or Stata V.17.

In Aim 2, first, we will use GLMM with the appropriate link function to examine associations between acute care utilisation and both patient and clinic covariates, which will facilitate our understanding of what may predict emergency room visits and hospitalisations. Given the count distributions and zero inflation of emergency visits and hospitalisations, we will use either Poisson or negative binomial regressions that may involve a zero-inflation component. This will be evaluated using the Vuong test. For these analyses, we will conduct two-group (ie, veterans detected versus not detected to have depression) individual-level interrupted time series analyses through segmented regressions on repeated monthly visit counts over 54 months (1 October 2018-31 March 2023), divided into the same three segments: pre-COVID, COVID, and through the end of the observation period. Second, to understand the impact on mortality, we will conduct age-adjusted Cox (proportional hazards) regression analyses to estimate death rates (all-cause and cause-specific deaths per 1000 deaths) between FY2019 and 2023 after adjusting for additional patient covariates (eg, physical and mental health diagnoses). Time to censoring or death was calculated from the date of depression screening until the end of the period of interest or death, whichever came first. We will use the direct method of standardisation separately for women and men, using the 2023 US population as the standard. To understand COVID-19 impacts, we will include a fixed effect for time with the three time segments. Finally, all models with psychiatric emergency/hospital visits outcomes and suicide mortality outcomes will be compared across veterans who screened positive and were detected versus not detected to have depression by clinicians. Examining trends against a counterfactual group of veterans who screened positive and were not detected to have depression may strengthen findings for our study cohort, or it may offer insight into veterans who may have been lost to follow-up (due to pandemic disruptions) and not detected at all. Again, the extremely large sample size allows for the detection of very small effect sizes in these regression models. For example, for a Cox regression model with a reasonable assumption on the R2 among the covariates with a specific predictor of 0.2, a HR of 1.02 with greater than 90% power (5% significance). This is a very small effect size, so clinically meaningful effects will be easy to detect. Even small differences detected will be clinically significant for adverse outcomes, such as mortality.
Qualitative data collection
Setting

For Aim 3, we will recruit VA providers and veterans from 3 VA healthcare systems (GLA, Syracuse and Durham). Sites were selected due to having varying size/complexity, telehealth use, patient population (eg, % women, % rural) and COVID-19 case rates (though peaks occurred during similar times) (online supplemental 6). The size and tenure of components of the sites' PCMHI programmes vary too, with CCC (CCC embeds PCMHI providers who are available for warm handoffs from primary care) and/or care management (CoCM offers phone-based depression care management by mental health-trained RNs). In FY2021, national VA averages were: 8% of primary care patients were seen by PCMHI providers; 31% of PCMHI occurred on the same day as primary care visits; 17% of patients have depression. Additionally, average wait times for new patients who need mental healthcare were at least 3 weeks at VA GLA, and shorter at VA Syracuse and Durham (1 week).
Participant characteristics

The total sample size of 80 (40 VA providers and 40 veteran patients) was selected to balance scientific yield with feasibility. Prior research suggests ~6 participants per subgroup is sufficient to reach saturation in theme identification.

VA provider interviews: in year 1, we will collect VA provider input on depression detection and management processes in primary care via interviews with approximately 40 VA primary care and PCMHI team members (ie, 6-8 from primary care and 4-8 from PCMHI for each of the 3 VA healthcare systems). Inclusion criteria are working as a VA primary care or PCMHI provider (eg, MD, PhD, RN) involved in depression detection and management in one of the 3 VA sites since the COVID-19 pandemic onset.

We will use purposive sampling, which emphasises selecting information-rich participants based on unique characteristics. Potential participants will be identified by operational partners and colleagues as subject matter experts, based on their clinical experience in primary care/PCMHI. Experts will include both staff and clinicians to reflect the range of providers involved in depression care processes (eg, nurses notify physicians of positive disease screen). We will present this research opportunity at appropriate clinical meetings and then send email invitations to participate. All individuals contacted will have the option to decline participation via email or phone. Unless an expert opts out, a research assistant will follow-up to ascertain willingness to participate, and if amenable, schedule the interview.

Veteran interviews: in year 2, we will gather input on pandemic-related care disruptions and preferred practices for hybrid in-person and telehealth depression care from veterans identified during quantitative data analyses. We will conduct interviews with 40 veteran patients (ie, 12-16 veterans total for each of the 3 VA healthcare systems). An RA will screen patients who contact the study for eligibility. For eligible patients (as specified below), the RA will explain the purpose of the interview, invite their participation, schedule the interview and administer a brief background survey with demographics.

Veteran inclusion criteria are primary care patients at one of the three VA healthcare systems, who have a positive depression screen (PHQ-2 >=3) in VA records over the past year, and have knowledge of their diagnosis. Eligible participants must respond affirmatively to the Behaviour Risk Factor Surveillance Survey question: 'has a doctor or other healthcare provider ever told you that you have a depressive disorder?'.

Using sequential mixed methods sampling, quantitative data from Aim 1 will be used to identify veterans who screened positive. We will stratify (ie, 50/50) veterans by whether or not clinicians had their depression during initial screening or subsequent VA encounters (ie, 6-8 detected and 6-8 undetected veterans from each site). Undetected veterans may have knowledge of their diagnosis if they were diagnosed in the past or diagnosed by non-VA providers. There is precedent and value in understanding the perspectives of patients with undetected needs in the VA. Interviewing both groups will inform us of differential patient experiences potentially related to pandemic disruption in clinical detection.

Since we will reach veterans who were not detected by clinicians to have depression, we will facilitate referrals for interested patients and work closely with local VA clinical teams where our study clinician-investigators are based. Our sampling strategy for veterans is not purposeful but instead based on criteria met in parallel work. We will mail recruitment letters that contain study information and contact options to opt out or for potential participation (ie, 1-800 phone number, email address). Because veterans who were not detected by clinicians may be difficult to reach compared with those who were detected, we plan to oversample the undetected cohort. To allow for exploratory analyses, we will ensure >=20% of participants are women and >=20% are racial-ethnic minorities, by oversampling during recruitment as needed.
Data collection procedures

Interviews with VA providers and veteran patients will be conducted using semistructured interview guides tailored for each group, with open-ended questions and probes as needed. Interview question development will be guided by Fortney et al's framework, which contains constructs that cannot be easily obtained using available administrative or medical records. The guide will include cross-cutting domains relevant to VA depression services for both types of interviews (eg, barriers and facilitators to care, assessment and treatment processes, timely care access). For example, VA providers will be asked about their perceptions of healthcare system-level determinants of care access (eg, work productivity with expanded telehealth) and potential best practices for team-based hybrid care models (eg, strategies for virtual handoffs) during the pandemic and beyond. Veterans with depression will be asked about perceived access to care, attitudes about care and need for care, which is critical to understand the extent to which changes in patient care-seeking behaviour account for any observed changes in healthcare utilisation during the pandemic. We will seek input from local Veteran Engagement Groups regarding interview design and content. Interviews will be conducted virtually (eg, phone, Microsoft Teams) and will last approximately 30 min for providers and 60 min for veterans. The interviewer will first read a consent script and then ask for verbal consent to participate and to be audio-recorded. If permissions are received, interviews will be digitally recorded and professionally transcribed. If a participant chooses not to be recorded, an RA will take detailed field notes manually. While non-employee veterans will receive US$50 incentives, providers will not be offered compensation due to the current VA policy.
Data analysis

Given the 2-year timeline of this study, we will use rapid qualitative analysis methods, which have been shown to save time and reduce costs while yielding valid results similar to those from traditional coding. We will expedite analyses by creating structured summaries for each interview using the transcript (or interview notes) according to core topics and constructs from Fortney et al's access framework covered in the interview guides. We will pilot the summary template with ~3 transcripts per participant type (Veteran, provider) to ensure analysts are using it consistently prior to dividing up transcripts. We will consolidate these summaries into a matrix by participant type, site and subgroups (veterans: detected, undetected; providers: PCMHI, primary care) to allow comparison across groups. We will identify key domains and broad themes (and subthemes within each) related to sources of disrupted care and actionable recommendations for future practice, triangulating across Veteran and provider interviews. Quantitative results will further inform matrix analysis to assess the depth and breadth of content on each topic. Given separate care delivery mechanisms for men and women (eg, women's clinics), we will also assess potential gender differences.
Discussion

There is widespread concern that the pandemic has negatively impacted the population's mental health and further speculation that veterans are especially vulnerable, given their baseline high rates of depression and loneliness/social isolation. Prior to the pandemic, the VA had made major strides toward universal depression and suicide-risk screening and invested heavily in primary care models to provide veterans with accessible treatment. Yet, quality gaps in depression follow-up and treatment remain staunchly in place and likely widened with COVID-19. Lost patient contacts with their primary care 'lifeline' have been substantiated by observed reductions in VA healthcare use. Correspondingly, there is concern for depression underdetection and undertreatment and its contributions to excess morbidity and mortality from suicidality and preventable medical disease. To our knowledge, no study has examined pandemic-related disruptions to VA depression care delivery and subsequent morbidity and mortality sequelae in the veteran population nationally.

At the same time, telehealth has rapidly expanded in an attempt to bridge access gaps widened by COVID-19, with little knowledge about the extent of its adoption and impact across both primary care and mental health services. Our study (in Aim 3) will secondarily close evidence gaps on patient and provider experiences from those who may not have initially elected to use telehealth, but were instead compelled to do so with COVID-19. Specifically, we will identify the ideal combination of virtual and in-person depression services for veterans at scale (eg, for whom, under what conditions) and provide the basis for testable hypotheses to improve hybrid (virtual/in-person) depression care delivery models (eg, enhanced by computerised psychotherapy) for at-scale dissemination through national primary care/PCMHI programme offices.

Our novel method in tracking a population's trajectory from a new positive depression (and suicide risk) screen to guideline-concordant follow-up and treatment in primary care/PCMHI team models with telehealth provides us with a solid framework for studying depression service interruptions among the entire VA population. This study is innovative in that it applies established quality indicators to a broad national scale at a critical time. We focus on practice changes during the COVID-19 pandemic, which could help provide important metrics to inform VA policy. Prior research has been conducted on only individuals coded with depression diagnoses and remains limited in scale:either large survey samples or regional administrative/electronic health record (EHR) datasets. The inclusion of providers and patients with and without detection of positive depression screening is another innovative feature. Given concern for veterans being lost to follow-up during the pandemic (and VA providers distracted from coding for depression due to competing pandemic-related demands), it is important to use alternative strategies to identify and then engage patients with mental health needs. For the first time, we will leverage a national disaster to naturally isolate modernisation strategies for depression care models and to deliver high-quality hybrid services to the entire VA population. Our study has the potential to help identify patients' specific needs and help clinics better address major challenges in care access.

In addition to its strengths, this study has some notable limitations. First, while an observational study precludes us from establishing causal relationships, associations noted will help us to better understand drivers of depression care quality improvement in the pandemic and eventual recovery. Quantitative analyses will have some unmeasured variables, such as primary care and mental health staffing and variable PCMHI implementation, which will then be addressed qualitatively. We will not have data on services provided by non-VA payors (eg, Medicare); however, the VA delivers the large majority of mental health services to veterans, as found in a previous study of veterans dually eligible to receive care in the VA and through Medicare. Second, qualitative analyses are limited by their focus on recruiting VA patients and providers from three specific VA sites, as opposed to sampling nationally. However, research is most likely to be successful at VA facilities where our study team is based, given our abilities to personally engage with involved veterans and local staff. Additionally, we will be able to integrate quantitative findings with Veteran and VA provider interview data at the three recruitment sites. We will also have a greater ability to newly connect veterans who were not otherwise detected to have depression with local care teams. Finally, our study is predicated on identifying and tracking outcomes among patients with positive depression screens and is inherently limited by the accuracy of the PHQ-2 screening tool and cut points established by VA clinical Practice Guidelines. Our research will, however, examine alternate PHQ-2 cut-points (eg, >=2) supported by new research and will likely assist with updates to future Clinical Practice Guidelines.
Ethics and dissemination

This study was reviewed by the VA GLA Healthcare System Institutional Review Board Administrator (IORG000133l) and determined to be exempt from the requirements of 38 Code of Federal Regulations 16 under Categories 2(iii) and 4(iii) (project #1714689). It was approved by the VA GLA Healthcare System Research and Development Committee on 15 March 2023.

Our dissemination plan will target research products to different audiences, including traditional academic products, briefings to our policy and operational partners, and presentations to clinical, research and policy-oriented audiences. We will also disseminate key conclusions and recommendations to the field, such as presentations at Community of Practice Calls and annual primary care/PCMHI training materials. Trainings would then reach VA providers nationwide with guidance on how to improve in-person and virtual depression care. Results will be disseminated to veterans/families in accordance with recommendations from our Veteran Engagement Group.

passages.text: Age-related aberrant alternative splicing as a prognostic tool in older breast cancer patients

Breast cancer is one of the most prevalent malignancies among women. Although the impact of age on breast cancer progression is well documented, the role of aberrant alternative splicing events in older adults breast cancer patients remains poorly understood. Here, we identified that older adults breast cancer patients exhibit a higher frequency of aberrant alternative splicing events compared to younger patients using public database, a finding that was further validated by data from FUSCC cohorts. A total of 390 high-variability-specific splicing events were observed exclusively in older adults patients. The unsupervised clustering analysis revealed the existence of three distinct subtypes of older adults patients, each displaying significantly different immune cell infiltration profiles and prognostic outcomes. To identify the key regulatory factors of these splicing subtypes, we conducted AS activity score analysis and identified 68 RNA-binding proteins as potential modulators. Subsequently, a machine learning approach using SelectKBest-SVM was employed to construct a predictive model, which demonstrated optimal performance in predicting the prognosis of older adults breast cancer patients, with a high AUC and validation on an independent test set. The developed predictive model offers a promising tool for personalized treatment strategies and accurate prognostication, advancing precision medicine for older adults breast cancer patients.

The frequency of aberrant alternative splicing events increases with age in breast cancer patients, including 390 high-variability-specific splicing events that are exclusively observed in older adults with breast cancer. Alternative splicing events can also be used to resolve three distinct subtypes of older adults with breast cancer, and predict the prognosis of older patients.
Introduction

Breast cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, ranking second among cancers in women, just behind lung cancer. It is well documented that age is a critical risk factor for the development of breast cancer. Both incidence and mortality rates increase markedly in individuals aged 65 years and above. The ageing global population has resulted in an increased prevalence of breast cancer in older adults women, emphasizing the necessity for more effective treatment strategies for this growing population. In fact, older adults patients often display distinct clinical and molecular characteristics compared to younger individuals, which can result in less effective treatment responses when standard therapeutic protocols are used. However, the specific molecular mechanisms contributing to the distinctive characteristics of breast cancer in older adults patients, particularly those involving age-related alterations, remain poorly understood.

One key regulatory process that contributes to these age-related differences is alternative splicing (AS), a post-transcriptional mechanism that generates protein diversity by selectively including or excluding exons from the mature mRNA. AS plays an essential role in numerous cellular processes, and its dysregulation is closely associated with cancer progression. Recent studies have shown that the frequency of aberrant AS events increases with age, and such alterations have been implicated in the development of various cancers, including breast cancer. Nevertheless, the characteristics of AS in older adults breast cancer patients have been unclear.

In this study, we demonstrate that older adults breast cancer patients exhibit a higher frequency of aberrant AS events compared to younger patients, suggesting that age-related changes in splicing contribute to the distinct clinical characteristics of older adults breast cancer. We identify 390 splicing events uniquely prevalent in older adults patients, which are associated with immune microenvironmental differences and prognosis. Furthermore, we identify 68 RNA-binding proteins that regulate these splicing events and construct a predictive machine learning model, which shows optimal accuracy in prognostic prediction for older adults patients. These findings provide a foundation for using AS and RBPs as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in personalized breast cancer treatment.

In this study, we downloaded clinical data and corresponding gene expression profiles of BRCA patients from the TCGA database. We collected 342 cancer samples and 31 adjacent normal samples from older adults breast cancer patients. To compare the number of AS abnormal events, we also collected 186 cancer samples and 31 adjacent normal samples from younger breast cancer patients. We downloaded the PSI matrix of AS data for BRCA patients from TCGASpliceSeq and ultimately organized a gene expression matrix for 31,529 genes and a PSI matrix for 13,479 AS events of 5685 genes. To examine whether there were differences in splicing patterns between cancer and normal samples that could facilitate the subsequent search for AS abnormal splicing events, we used t-SNE dimensionality reduction clustering visualization with PSI values associated with each AS event (Fig. 1A). The t-SNE visualization results indicated apparent differences in splicing patterns between normal and cancer samples. To minimize analytical interference, six samples with discrete value (three aged tissues and three young tissues) were excluded from subsequent analyses (see Discussion section). After screening, we finally obtained 340 cancer samples (n = 340) and 30 adjacent normal samples (n = 30) in the older adults group; in the young group, we obtained 184 cancer samples (n = 184) and 30 adjacent normal samples (n = 30) (Supplementary Data 1). We then used t-SNE for visualization again and confirmed that after the removal of the abnormal samples, the t-SNE clustering results more clearly distinguished between normal and cancer samples (Fig. 1B, C). We used t-tests to identify AS abnormal splicing events in both the older adults and young groups (Supplementary Data 2-3). The results showed that although there was no apparent difference in the proportion of AS abnormal splicing event types between the two groups (Fig. 1D), the older adults group had a higher number of abnormal splicing events overall (Fig. 1E). To test the accuracy of the differential analysis and explore its biological relevance, we confirmed the intersection of differential splicing events from both groups (Fig. 1F), of which 643 intersection differential splicing events involved 561 genes (Fig. 1G) and were significantly enriched in pathways related to cell-substrate junction (Fisher's exact test, P < 0.05) and focal adhesion (Fisher's exact test, P < 0.05), which are directly or closely linked to tumor progression (Fig. 1H). Among the 643 intersection differential splicing events, there are many variable splicing events that have been experimentally confirmed and proven to be closely related to the occurrence and progression of cancer, such as the variable splicing of GNAS, which was found and confirmed to be closely related to the occurrence of breast cancer in previous reports. These results indicate the commonality of the intersection abnormal splicing events in driving the occurrence and progression of breast cancer in the two groups. The visualization of t-SNE dimensionality reduction clustering of all differential splicing events (abnormal splicing events in the older adults and young breast cancer patients, Supplementary Data 2 and 3) in the two groups (Fig. S2A). To investigate age-related splicing alterations in breast cancer, we analyzed AS events in older adults patients. A heatmap visualizing older adults-specific PSI values revealed different splicing patterns between tumor and adjacent normal tissues in the older adults cohort (Fig. S2B). To further investigate whether these older adults-specific splicing events could distinguish tumor from normal tissue within the older adults group, we performed t-SNE analysis. The result demonstrated clear segregation between tumor and normal tissue samples in the older adults patients based on their older adults-specific splicing profiles (Fig. S2C). Similarly, we assessed the mRNA expression levels of these older adults-specific splicing events using t-SNE. In contrast to the splicing profiles, gene expression patterns showed unfavorable separation between tumor and normal tissues in the older adults patients (Fig. S2C).

To validate the observation that older adults breast cancer patients exhibit a higher frequency of aberrant splicing events, we analyzed the data using an independent tool, TCGA_SpIAdder. Consistent with our SpliceSeq findings, TCGA_SpIAdder analysis revealed more aberrant splicing events in older patients compared to younger patients (Fig. S4A, S4B).Moreover, in FUSCC cohort, we independently validated findings using rMATS, MISO, and SUPPA2 tools. Analysis with rMATS (Fig. S4C, upper), MISO (Fig. S4C, lower), and SUPPA2 (Fig. S4D, S4E) confirmed an increased prevalence of aberrant AS events in older patients.

Exploring high-variability-specific (HVS) splicing events and the splicing factors that drive them in this population could better represent the older adults and hold important clinical relevance. Splicing events with high variance have a substantial impact on the overall splicing landscape. By using a threshold of std_psi > 0.15 to identify high-variance splicing events, we identified 390 such events (Fig. 1I and Supplementary Data 4). These events were visualized using t-SNE clustering (Fig. 1J), which demonstrated that they could distinguish two distinct types of samples within the older adults group but lacked similar representativeness in the young group. A heatmap of PSI values further confirmed that these splicing events are more representative in older adults breast cancer patients. Among the 390 splicing events with high variability, most showed significantly different PSI levels compared to normal tissues (Wilcoxon test, P < 0.05) (Fig. 1I and Fig. S3B). These events involved 326 genes (Supplementary Data 5) and covered a variety of splicing event types (Figure S3A).

To further explore these findings, we conducted univariate Cox regression analysis to select the top ten splicing event genes with potential prognostic relevance, involving thirteen splicing events (Fig. S3C and Supplementary Table 1). Additionally, we experimentally validated the specificity of these splicing events in the older adults breast cancer population. We conducted experimental confirmation of the specificity of some of these splicing events in the older adults population. We designed specific primers targeting these splicing events (Fig. 1K, see Methods for details) and analyzed samples from the Ganzhou cohort, dividing them into young and older adults groups for RT-qPCR experiments. The results demonstrated that these splicing events occurred at significantly higher frequencies in the older adults group (Student's t test, P < 0.05), confirming their specific presence in this population (Fig. 1L). Based on univariate Cox regression analysis and experimental validation results, we found several aberrant splicing events with high incidence in the older adults population, which may be closely associated with their prognosis. These findings provide important insights into the biological relevance of older adults-specific abnormal splicing events and lay a foundation for further exploration of their role in the prognosis of the older adults population.
Unsupervised clustering analysis revealed three different splicing patterns in older adults breast cancer patients according to HVS splicing events in the older adults

In older adults breast cancer patients, more abnormal AS event disorder occurs, and different patients show varying degrees of splicing pattern disorder. According to the similarity of splicing patterns, older adults breast cancer patients can be further divided into multiple subtypes. To more accurately explore and analyze these subtypes, we applied non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) clustering, based on the percentage splicing index (PSI) values of the high-variability specific (HVS) splicing events, to cluster analysis of older adults BRCA patients. Through multiple repetitions of clustering, the optimal number of clusters was determined to be K = 3 (Fig. 2A), and finally, 340 older adults BRCA patients were divided into three AS splicing patterns, named AS Cluster1 (n = 85), AS Cluster2 (n = 156), and AS Cluster3 (n = 99) (Fig. 2B). T-SNE (t-distribution stochastic neighbor embedding) results further verified the validity of this classification (Fig. 2C). Subsequently, we conducted survival analysis on the three types of patients to explore the differences in their clinical prognosis. The three splicing patterns showed significant survival differences (log-rank test, P < 0.05) in overall survival (OS) (Fig. 2D). Among them, AS Cluster1 showed a clear survival advantage, while AS Cluster3 had dismal survival prognosis. In disease-free survival (DFS) analysis, AS Cluster3 also showed dismal survival prognosis (log-rank test, P < 0.05) (Fig. S5A). This finding prompted us to delve deeper into the molecular differences among the three splicing patterns. We further compared the differences among the three clusters in terms of breast cancer IHC classification and PAM50 typing (Fig. 2E). The results indicated that patients in Cluster3 were more likely to exhibit the most malignant molecular subtype:triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). This finding is consistent with the previous prognosis analysis, which suggested that patients in Cluster3 have the most dismal prognosis in clinical settings. In addition, in TNM staging analysis, the proportion of N2/N3 in Cluster3 patients in lymph node (Node) staging was significantly higher (Fisher's exact test, P < 0.05) than in the other two clusters, indicating that these patients may be more prone to local and distant lymph node metastasis (Fig. S5B). However, there were no significant differences (Fisher's exact test, P > 0.05) among the three groups in tumor primary site (T stage) and distant metastasis (M stage). To provide a more detailed of the characteristics distinguishing the different clusters, we further analyzed the tumor microenvironment and genomic instability among the clusters. This is further reflected in the hypoxia scores, with Cluster3 exhibiting significantly higher hypoxia levels across all three scoring systems: Buffa, Winter, and Ragnum, indicating a more hypoxic tumor microenvironment (Fig. 2F). Moreover, Cluster3 exhibited significantly higher (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05) Aneuploidy scores (Fig. S5C), indicative of strong genomic instability. Further supporting this, higher Fraction Genome Altered scores (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05) suggest that Cluster3 is characterized by a genomic landscape dominated by chromosomal instability (Fig. S5C). Moreover, we analyzed the H&E staining results in the TCGA cohort to explore the tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) levels in the three types of patients. The results showed that the TIL levels in Cluster3 patients were significantly higher (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05) than in other groups (Fig. 2G, H), we also further show the representative H&E staining and its statistical data (Fig. 2H). While the TIL levels and the proportion of high-TILs areas in Cluster1 were lower. Studies have shown that an increase in TIL proportion is usually associated with prolonged survival in HER2-positive or TNBC patients; however, in HER2-negative ductal breast cancer patients, a high TIL proportion is a negative prognostic factor, indicating that different subtypes of breast cancer may have different immune response patterns. Although patients in Cluster3 have a high TIL level and a higher proportion of TNBC subtype patients, theoretically, their survival should be extended, but the actual results are not the case. These findings prompted us to further explore the differences in the tumor immune microenvironment among the three clusters to reveal potential molecular mechanisms.
Three different splicing patterns exhibit distinct immune landscapes and molecular features
Different TME and Signaling Pathway Characteristics of the Three AS RNA Processing Patterns.

We used the ESTIMATE method to estimate the overall levels of immune cell and stromal cell infiltration in older adults breast cancer samples (Fig. 3A-C). Notably, compared to AS Cluster1 and AS Cluster2, AS Cluster3 showed increased immune scores and increased stromal scores (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05), but lower tumor purity, indicating a higher level of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in the Cluster3 subtype. Cluster1 had higher immune scores than Cluster2, while Cluster2 had higher stromal scores than Cluster1. The higher immune score in Cluster1 suggests a stronger immune response in its tumor microenvironment, which may be associated with more favorable survival prognosis. Cluster2, with a higher stromal score and the highest tumor purity among the patients, indicates a rich stromal component in the tumor microenvironment, with tumor cells dominating the microenvironment, which may promote tumor invasiveness and metastasis, leading to more dismal prognosis. To compare the differences in TME cell infiltration between clusters, we comprehensively assessed the TME infiltration patterns in older adults breast cancer patients. As shown in Fig. 3D, cells, such as Memory B cells and Monocytes exhibited higher levels of infiltration in AS Cluster1 (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05), which may lead to stronger immune surveillance and anti-tumor responses, thus improving prognosis. Although AS Cluster3 was in a state of high immune infiltration, they may be functionally exhausted and unable to effectively combat the tumor, resulting in a more dismal prognosis. We further compared the differences in immune-related gene set scores among the three splicing subtypes in terms of immune checkpoints, antigen processing mechanisms, CD8 T effector features and EMT marker gene sets, including EMT1, EMT2, and EMT3, were highest in Cluster3, suggesting its tumor cells have stronger invasive and metastatic abilities (Fig. 3E). In summary, the AS Cluster3 subtype with high immune infiltration may be more prone to metastasis. HLA genes play a key role in antigen presentation and immune recognition, and their expression can influence the immune response in the tumor microenvironment. Therefore, we compared the expression of HLA family genes among the three clusters. Cluster3 showed higher expression of multiple HLA genes (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05), indicating active antigen presentation, although high HLA gene expression is typically associated with a stronger immune response, in Cluster3, combined with the high expression of immune checkpoint genes, it may suggest that the tumor activates the HLA pathway while also evading immune surveillance through other means(Fig. 3F). Finally, we used various deconvolution algorithm methods, such as Quantiseq, Timer, MCP_counter, and Xcell to calculate the levels of immune cell infiltration in breast cancer samples using RNA-seq data, further demonstrating the high infiltration level of Cluster3 (Fig. S6A). Additionally, there were significant differences (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05) in mRNA expression of immune checkpoints between clusters (Fig. S6B). To reveal possible T cell exhaustion in Cluster3, we examined the expression of exhaustion-related genes, such as LAG3, TIGIT, LAYN, PDCD1, HAVCR2, and CXCL13 in the three splicing subtypes, and these marker genes were all highly expressed (Kruskal-Wallis test, P < 0.05) in Cluster3 (Figs. 3G and S6C-S6E), further suggesting the possibility of T cell exhaustion in this cluster.
Mutational characteristics of splicing pattern clusters

Subsequently, to further characterize and discuss the mechanisms of the three splicing patterns, we performed gene set variation analysis (GSVA). We first compared the pathways upregulated in each of the three clusters: in Fig. 3H, Cluster1 showed higher enrichment in signaling pathways, such as INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE, E2F TARGETS, and MTORC1 SIGNALING; Cluster2 showed relatively neutral or slightly downregulated pathways, but the upregulation of its ESTROGEN RESPONSE LATE pathway indicated increased sensitivity to estrogen signaling, which may be related to tumor proliferation, metabolic activation, and sensitivity to hormone therapy. Cluster3 showed higher enrichment in pathways related to metabolism, cell proliferation, and oxidative phosphorylation. Next, we compared the pathways downregulated in each cluster (Fig. 3I). In Cluster3, we particularly noted immune-related signaling pathways, such as INTERFERON GAMMA RESPONSE and INTERFERON ALPHA RESPONSE, which are closely related to immune responses. The downregulation of interferon signaling pathways may imply a poorer response to viral and anti-tumor immunity in Cluster3. Additionally, the downregulation of the IL6_JAK_STAT3_SIGNALING pathway suggests possible immune suppression or a reduction in inflammatory responses in Cluster3. Through GSEA analysis, we found that Cluster1 exhibited strong activity in antigen processing and presentation pathways, suggesting higher immune activity, which may contribute to a more favorable prognosis. The enrichment of the HIF-1 signaling pathway in Cluster2 suggests enhanced tumor cell adaptation to hypoxic conditions, further promoting tumor survival and spread. In Cluster3, the enrichment of the ECM receptor interaction pathway also suggests potential invasiveness and migratory ability of tumor cells. In addition, we conducted GO enrichment analysis for the differentially expressed genes in each subtype compared to the other two subtypes (Fig. S6F-S6H), further validating the differences in pathway mechanisms mentioned above. In summary, we propose to name Cluster1 the Immune Enhancement type, Cluster2 the Hormone Activation type, and Cluster3, which exhibits enhanced metabolism and invasiveness, the Metabolic Invasion type. We next performed the GSEA enrichment analysis to further demonstrate the characteristic pathways of each cluster (Fig. 3J).

AS events are primarily regulated by RNA-Binding Protein (RBPs). RBPs typically bind to precursor mRNA and regulate RNA splicing by influencing the selection of exons and splice sites. Further exploration of the RBP-AS regulatory network will help understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of BRCA and provide potential targets for precision therapy. Therefore, in this study, exploring the regulatory network between RBPs and AS events is of great importance. To determine the molecular regulators associated with the 390 high-variability specific (HVS) splicing events, We first determined the extent of perturbation of these HVS splicing events by comparing the PSI (splicing percentage index) for each splicing event with the normal sample(Fig. 5A). We calculated two activity scores for these splicing events: an activation activity score (SA) and a suppression activity score (SR), ultimately identifying 201 over-activated and 189 over-suppressed splicing events. We then manually collected 2217 RBPs as candidate regulators of splicing events(Supplementary Data 6). Next, we determined the potential RBP regulators of AS events in different cancer types based on the correlation between the expression of candidate regulators and AS activity scores (Fig. 5B). In total, we found 1552 RBPs positively correlated with the activation score and 1450 RBPs positively correlated with the suppression score in over-activated splicing events (Fig. 5C, D, and Supplementary Data 7-8). Given the adverse prognostic nature of Cluster3 in our earlier analyses, we focused on splicing factors abnormally expressed in Cluster3. Ultimately, we identified 68 differentially expressed splicing factors (Wilcoxon test, P < 0.05) in Cluster3 (Fig. 5E, F). Nine of these splicing factors were activating RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) (Fig. 5E), and 59 were inhibitory RBPs (Fig. 5F). Each of these factors was predicted to regulate at least 30 of the 390 HVSs (Supplementary Data 7 and 8), based on previously identified molecular regulators associated with HVSs (Fig. 5A-D). Representative examples illustrated the relationship between HVS splicing events and specific splicing factors (Fig. 5G).

We believe that these potential splicing factors may indeed be able to predict splicing pattern subtypes and prognosis in the older adults population. We attempted to construct a classifier that could distinguish between Cluster3 and Non-Cluster3. Using these potential splicing factors, we built a machine learning model, and after feature selection and classifier construction (Fig. 6A), we systematically evaluated 50 combinations of feature selection methods and machine learning algorithms. Model performance was assessed using metrics including Area Under the Curve (AUC) (Fig. 6B, S7A-D) and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) (Fig. 6C). Thirteen models demonstrated strong performance, with AUC > 0.75 and MCC > 0.4. These included SelectKBest-LR, SelectKBest-GP, SelectKBest-KNN, SelectKBest-SVM, RFE_RF-GP, RFE_RF-DA, RFE_RF-SVM, SelectFromModel_LR-KNN, SelectFromModel_RF-LR, SelectFromModel_RF-GP, SelectFromModel_RF-DA, SelectFromModel_RF-DT, and SelectFromModel_RF-RF. To validate our findings externally, we considered the METABRIC dataset, a comprehensive, publicly available breast cancer resource containing clinical and molecular data from over 2000 patients. Results indicated that only the SelectKBest-SVM model demonstrated satisfactory performance (Fig. 6D, Supplementary Table 2). Further validation using independent datasets (GSE42568 and GSE20685) consistently revealed that the SelectKBest-SVM model predicted a significantly poorer prognosis for patients in Cluster3 (log-rank P < 0.05) (Fig. 6E, F, Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, other models with similar cross-validation metrics failed to consistently predict prognosis robustly. The poor prognostic signature associated with Cluster3 was further validated in an independent GSE25066 external dataset (Fig. S7E). Finally, we confirmed SelectKBest-SVM as the optimal classifier.

We applied this classifier to our Ganzhou cohort to predict the subtypes to which patients might belong. First we confirmed by H&E staining results that older breast cancer patients predicted as Cluster3 subtype indeed had higher TIL levels (Fig. 6G). In addition, by comparing the abnormal splicing events in the older adults group and the abnormal splicing events in the younger group in the Ganzhou cohort, Fig. 6H demonstrated representative examples with split-read counts and exon quantification data. ADAM15 exhibited increased the proportion of exon exclusion in Cluster3, while CCDC88B displayed decreased the proportion of exon exclusion. These directional changes were independently validated using MISO (Fig. S8A), confirming their consistency with rMATS outputs (Fig. 6H).

To provide an isoform-level interpretation of AS changes, we employed IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR to identify differential isoform switching between Cluster3 and Non-Cluster3 groups (Fig. S8B). KEGG enrichment analysis further revealed that genes undergoing significant isoform switching were associated with tumor-related pathways, including cell adhesion and p53 signaling (Fig. S8C).Significant isoform switches were observed in key genes, including MGP and ARHGDIA. In Cluster3, MGP exhibited a pronounced shift from the full-length transcript ENST00000228938.5 (encoding the functional Gla domain) to the truncated isoform ENST00000545199.5, which lacks exons 1, 2, and 4 (Fig. S8D). Similarly, ARHGDIA showed decreased expression of the functional transcript ENST00000541078.7 and increased expression of the NMD-sensitive isoform ENST00000582520.1 (Fig. S8E). We further analyzed differential exon usage in RNA-seq data using DEXSeq, which revealed significant exon usage differences for the genes MGP (ENSG00000111341) and ARHGDIA (ENSG00000141522) between Cluster3 and Non-Cluster3 (Fig. S8F).

We also performed preliminary qPCR experiments at the protein level on the 10 RBPs that were eventually used for model construction, such as SNRNP70 low expression of activating RBPs in patients judged to be Cluster3, and other RBPs also showed the accuracy of the previous analysis on the overall trend (Fig. 6I).

To explore the application of our developed classifier in single-cell data, we collected single-cell sequencing data from breast cancer patients over the age of 65 and conducted integrated analysis. Through cell annotation, we ultimately identified various cell types (Fig. 6J and S9A). We next compared the difference in the proportion of cell types predicted as Cluster3 and those predicted as Non-Cluster3, where Cluster3 exhibited more T cell proportions (Fig. 6K and S9B). Since we had previously discussed the immune-related characteristics of Cluster3 in detail, we next focused on the T cell subpopulations. After annotating the T cell subpopulations, we determined several T cell subgroups, including Activated T cell, Cytotoxic T cell, Exhausted T cell, Naive, Prolifrerating, Thf, Treg (Fig. 6L and S9C). Then, we applied the classifier to determine the subtype affiliation of these cells (Fig. S9D). We analyzed the proportions of different T cell types across all samples in both groups. The results revealed a higher proportion of exhausted T cells in Cluster3 (15.8% VS 6.3%, chi-square tests, P < 2.2e-16) compared to the Non-Cluster3 group (Fig. 6M). This finding aligns with our previous results, which showed increased expression of immun e exhaustion-related genes in Cluster3 from RNA-seq data (Figs. 3G and S6C-S6E).
